newsitem.title: ERITREA: Eritrea sees big export potential in salt.
newsitem.headline: Eritrea sees big export potential in salt.

text.p: Salt offers Eritrea its best hope of increasing exports, Alem Tzehay of the Ministry of Trade and Industry told Reuters in an interview.
"It (salt) is our potential commodity. What we produce in big quantity is that one only. We are starting to export to the Comesa (Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa) area", Alem said.

"The Red Sea coast is famous for its salt. We feel we have some of the best salt in the Red Sea", said Michael Tsegai, an engineer with the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), working on the rehabilitation of the country's salt works.
Eritrea has two major salt works, in the coastal cities of Massawa and Assab, both started by Italians during the colonial era.
Since the war with Ethiopia ended in 1991, money has been spent on rehabilitating the two salt works and they have recently been added to the government's list of industries to be privatised in 1997.

According to the ministry, Eritrean salt was exported during the 1960s and 70s to the Far East, the Middle East, East African and Southern African countries. When the war with Ethiopia intensified in the 70s exports stopped and all output was sold domestically.
"Until last year, all the salt went to domestic Eritrean supplies and to Ethiopia. In 1996 we started to export salt to East African countries", said Michael Tsegai.
In 1996 some 8,000 tonnes of salt were exported to Kenya and Tanzania, about half the total exports for the year.
He said that between 1992 and 1996, the Eritrean government invested 32 million birr ($5.0 million) in the Massawa salt works and 12 million birr at Assab.

The money was used for a washing plant and iodisation plant and the rehabilitation of industrial and social buildings in Massawa, and new machinery, rehabilitation of existing salt fields and infrastructure in Assab, he said.
The salt fields at Massawa total 330 hectares, with annual capacity of 80,000 tonnes and production now running at about 80 percent, ccording to MTI.
The productive area at the Assab salt works is 250 hectares. Capacity is 180,000 tonnes a year and production is 150,000 tonnes a year, according to MTI.
"The wind is stronger, the humidity is lower and the soil structure is better in Assab", Michael said.
The Massawa salt works sold eight million birr worth of salt in 1996. Assab sales totalled 27 million birr.
Michael said he wants to see more salt works in Eritrea:
"We have invited English consultants, Manderstam Consulting Services, to do a feasibility study for salt works in both the private and public sector in all Eritrea.

"The final report is expected in June. We will have more salt works, especially in the private sector. We want to encourage small private businesses. Now, families around Massawa are producing salt with very primitive techniques. We will give them some technical aid so that they can improve the quality".

"We are looking at the export potential around the world. We think we have a big potential. We feel that we can increase sales by 20 to 25 percent in the next three to four years", said Michael Tsegai.

"We hope we will have a good market in these (Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa) areas. Especially the landlocked countries. South Africa is the only real competitor", said Alem Tzehay, head of Trade at the MTI.
He said other products with export potential included fish, gum arabic, hides and footwear. ($=6.4 birr)
